what: the two published brains, rebuilt from their public sources and compared to the chain
why: Every other check on the brains starts from bytes somebody is already serving -- Greenfield, the Cloudflare mirror, a peer's tab. All of those can go away. This one starts from the public record instead, and asks whether the content address can be reconstructed by anyone who has the papers.

inputs.note: downloaded fresh over the public internet; nothing from this project, its buckets or its mirrors was used

rebuilt.name: flywire-fafb-v783-min2
rebuilt.note: this is the base every individual is laid out on

onchain.checked: exists(bytes32) and claimBinding(bytes32) for each rebuilt mepId

conclusion: Both brains were reproduced byte-for-byte from public inputs in under 17 seconds each, and each rebuild's mepId is registered on BSC testnet against the same modelId. Nothing this project hosts was needed to get there.
limits: This reproduces the BASE brains. The 100 founders are 228-byte deltas ON that base; a delta is only as recoverable as the place it was published to (Greenfield, today).
The name is part of the payload's bytes: only --name flywire-fafb-v783-min5 / -min2 give these addresses. An otherwise identical export under another name is a different brain.
Zenodo and the annotations repo are themselves single points -- what this shows is that the INPUTS are public and the transform is deterministic, not that any particular host will stay up.
